204.title: The snake-catcher
204.hook: a man hauls a frozen dragon into Baghdad, and the sun thaws it (Masnavi 3.976ff)
204.howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, the nafs, the self that grasps, is watched with care, and this story is often told to warn that a desire that seems gone may only be waiting for opportunity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the man who stopped calling learned the call is the answer. Your line again. What did you keep doing without a sign? Day two hundred four.

Someone says: oh, I don't really have a temper anymore. Or: I'm totally over that. Or: I could stop anytime. And it's true, as far as they know. It's been quiet for months. Then comes the holiday with the family, or the bonus check, or the night alone with nothing to do, and there it is again, bigger than before. It wasn't gone. It was cold. Rumi tells a story about a man who made exactly that mistake, and got very rich for about an hour. Today: the snake-catcher.
screen: `I'M TOTALLY OVER THAT.` → `IT WASN'T GONE. IT WAS COLD.` → `THE SNAKE-CATCHER.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Three of the Masnavi. A snake-catcher, a man who made his living catching snakes and showing them off, goes up into the mountains in winter looking for a good one. And he finds a monster: an enormous dragon, lying frozen in the snow. It doesn't move. It seems dead. What a find! He drags it all the way down to Baghdad to put it on show. Word spreads that a snake-catcher has brought in a dragon, and huge crowds come to the riverbank to see it. He's wrapped it up in ropes and heavy cloth, and he waits for the crowd to get bigger. It's worth waiting for. But the sun of Iraq is warm. It shines on the dragon. The cold slowly leaves its body. It starts to stir. The ropes snap. The crowd panics and runs, and many are hurt in the crush. The snake-catcher stands frozen with fear, and the dragon swallows him. Then Rumi turns to the reader. Your lower self is that dragon, he says. The Sufi word is nafs: the grasping, angry, hungry part of us. How could it be dead? It's only frozen, by lack of means, by having no chance to act. Keep it in the snow, Rumi warns. Don't carry it into the sun of Iraq. The sun is opportunity: money, power, freedom, the right moment. It's worth hearing that Rumi doesn't say the snake-catcher was evil. He was proud, a little greedy, and wrong about what was dead. Knowing your dragon isn't shameful. Parading it around thinking it's harmless is where the trouble starts. Your line: careful in the sun.
screen: `A FROZEN DRAGON IN THE SNOW.` · `DRAGGED TO BAGHDAD FOR A SHOW.` · `THE SUN OF IRAQ WAKES IT.` · then, large: `CAREFUL IN THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one frozen dragon in you. Settle, and ask kindly: what's quiet in me only because it hasn't had a chance? A temper, a craving, a grudge, an old habit. Name it, without shame. Then ask: what's the sun that would wake it? Too much money, too little sleep, a certain person, a certain night. Just know it's there. The bell holds the time.
The snake-catcher. A man drags a frozen dragon into Baghdad to show it off, and the warm sun brings it back to life. Today's word.
Your line: careful in the sun. Today, stay a step away from the sun you named: one less drink, one skipped scroll, one conversation left for tomorrow. Day two hundred four.

205.title: The same reason then
205.hook: don't be troubled by the future; you'll meet it with the same reason you have now (Meditations 7.8)
205.howItsDone: Many readers of the Stoics use this line at night or in anxious moments, reminding themselves that the same judgment and care they have today will be there when the future arrives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the snake-catcher and his frozen dragon, woken by the sun. Your line was careful in the sun. Did you stay a step away from yours? Day two hundred five.

It's 2am. The house is quiet, and your mind is running a movie of next month. The meeting where it all goes wrong. The bill you can't pay. The phone call from the doctor. You play it three different ways, and every version, you're alone and unprepared. Here's the strange thing: in the movie, the person facing the future is a weaker, more confused version of you. Somehow we imagine that when the hard day comes, we'll show up with nothing. Marcus had a short answer to 2am. Today: the same reason then.
screen: `2AM, THE MOVIE OF NEXT MONTH.` → `A WEAKER VERSION OF YOU.` → `THE SAME REASON THEN.`

segments.voice: Book Seven, section eight, in George Long's translation: "Let not future things disturb thee, for thou wilt come to them, if it shall be necessary, having with thee the same reason which now thou usest for present things." Look at the three pieces. First: let not future things disturb you. Not: the future won't be hard. It might be. Just: don't let it trouble you now. Second: if it shall be necessary. A lot of what we dread never arrives. Marcus doesn't promise that, but he leaves the door open. Third, the heart of it: you'll bring with you the same reason you're using today. Reason, for the Stoics, meant more than logic. It meant the whole power in you to see clearly, choose well and act rightly. And it's portable. You carry it everywhere. Whatever you use today to handle the dishes, the emails and the hard conversation, you'll have tomorrow too. The 2am movie always forgets this. It sends a helpless you into the future. Marcus says it'll be the same you, with the same tools, and probably more practice. And that gathers up our week of seeing clearly. The purple robe was only wool and shellfish. The emperor refused to be dyed a Caesar. The bee belongs to the hive. Our palms are small on the elephant. The call was already the answer. The dragon was only frozen. And the future is met by the same mind you have now. Your line: the same reason then.
screen: `LET NOT FUTURE THINGS DISTURB THEE.` · `IF IT SHALL BE NECESSARY.` · `THE SAME REASON YOU USE NOW.` · then, large: `THE SAME REASON THEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave one future worry for later. Settle, and let one worry about the future come up. Look at it once. Then picture yourself, on that day, with the same mind and the same care you have right now, maybe with a friend beside you. Say inside: I'll meet it then. And set it down for these two minutes. If it comes back, just say it again. The bell holds the time.
The same reason then. Marcus says don't be troubled by the future: you'll meet it with the same reason you use today. Today's word.
Your line: the same reason then. Today, when the worry comes back, say the line and turn to the thing in front of you right now. Day two hundred five.

206.title: Dig within
206.hook: within is the fountain of good, and it bubbles up if you keep digging (Meditations 7.59)
206.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often treat this line as a call to daily reflection, a few minutes of looking inward each morning or evening, as Marcus himself seems to have done in writing his notes.

segments.voice: Last week ended with Marcus at 2am, saying you'll meet the future with the same reason you have now. Your line was the same reason then. Did a worry wait its turn? Day two hundred six.

When you're running on empty, where do you go? Most of us go out. Another coffee. A pep talk video. A friend who'll tell us we're doing great. A new book promising the secret. None of that is bad. But it's like carrying water in cups from someone else's tap. It runs out, and you're back at the door. A new week starts today. It's called cooked, and it's about what happens to us under heat. But first, Marcus points somewhere we forget to look for water. Today: dig within.
screen: `RUNNING ON EMPTY.` → `WATER FROM SOMEONE ELSE'S TAP.` → `DIG WITHIN.`

segments.voice: It's one of the shortest entries in Book Seven. In George Long's translation: "Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig." Picture a well in a dry country. The water is there, underground, but you won't see it from the surface. You have to dig. And then, once you reach it, you keep the well clear, or the sand fills it in again. For Marcus the fountain is the part of you that can reason, choose and do good. The Stoics believed every human being carries a spark of the same reason that orders the universe. So the good isn't something you have to buy, borrow or earn from outside. It's already down there. Notice two small words in the line: ever, twice. It will ever bubble up, if you will ever dig. It's a promise with a condition. The spring doesn't run dry, but the digging never finishes. You don't dig once and live off it forever. You dig this morning, and again tonight. Many traditions share a picture like this. Jesus speaks of a spring of water welling up inside. The Upanishads talk of the self hidden in the heart. We'll let each keep its own meaning. For Marcus, it's plain and practical: when you need patience, courage or kindness, don't only look for someone to hand it to you. Look down. It's closer than you think. Your line: dig within.
screen: `WITHIN IS THE FOUNTAIN OF GOOD.` · `A WELL IN A DRY COUNTRY.` · `EVER BUBBLE UP, IF YOU EVER DIG.` · then, large: `DIG WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit and dig. Settle, and let your attention go down, below the noise of the day, the way a bucket goes down a well. Ask quietly: what's good in me right now? Patience, a little warmth, a steadiness, even just being awake. Don't force it. Keep digging gently, breath by breath. If you like, keep digging for a third minute after the bell. The bell holds the time.
Dig within. Marcus wrote that within you is a fountain of good that will always bubble up if you always dig. Today's word.
Your line: dig within. Today, when you reach for something outside to feel better, pause once and look down first. Day two hundred six.

screen: `DAY 206 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CHICKPEA IN THE POT.`

207.title: The chickpea in the pot
207.hook: a chickpea leaps from the boiling pot, and the cook says the heat is making it good (Masnavi 3.4158ff)
207.howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, the path is often described as moving from raw to cooked, and stories like this are told to help people bear hard training and change with patience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus said within is the fountain of good, if you keep digging. Your line was dig within. What did you find down there? Day two hundred seven.

Think of the hardest year you've had that you're now, oddly, glad of. The first job where you knew nothing. The move to a city where you knew no one. The year of the new baby, the long illness, the exam you had to retake. At the time it felt like being boiled alive. And yet something in you got softer, deeper, more you. Rumi often reached for pictures from the kitchen, and he wrote about a small, hard, dried-out bean that did not want to be in the pot. Today: the chickpea in the pot.
screen: `A HARD YEAR YOU'RE GLAD OF.` → `BOILED ALIVE, THEN SOFTER.` → `THE CHICKPEA IN THE POT.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Three of the Masnavi. Look at a chickpea in the pot, Rumi says, how it leaps up when the fire's lit. It keeps bobbing to the top, crying out: why are you setting me on fire? You bought me, and now you're turning me upside down! And the cook, a woman in Rumi's telling, keeps tapping it back down with her ladle. Boil nicely, she says. Don't jump away from the one who lit the fire. I'm not boiling you because I dislike you. It's so you'll get taste and flavor, so you can become food and mingle with life itself. Then she reminds the chickpea where it came from. When you were green and fresh in the garden, you drank the rain. That drinking was for the sake of this fire. And the chickpea, in the end, says: all right, then. If that's how it is, I'll boil gladly. Help me. Rumi is talking about the soul, and about the hard things a person goes through on the way to God. Sufis often speak of the raw and the cooked. A raw person is hard, dry, self-protective. A cooked one has been softened and made nourishing. It's worth being careful with this story. Rumi is talking about the heat that ripens: effort, change, loss, long training. He isn't saying you should stay where someone is harming you and call it cooking. Not all fire is a kitchen fire. But some of the heat in your life, the kind that's making you more patient, humbler, kinder, might be doing what the cook says. Your line: being cooked.
screen: `A CHICKPEA LEAPS FROM THE POT.` · `I'M NOT BOILING YOU OUT OF DISLIKE.` · `THE RAW AND THE COOKED.` · then, large: `BEING COOKED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one heat that's cooking you. Settle, and let one difficulty come to mind. Not the worst thing, and not anything where someone is hurting you. Something that's stretching you: a new role, a hard habit to build, a slow recovery. Feel the heat of it for a breath or two. Then ask gently: what might this be softening in me? The bell holds the time.
The chickpea in the pot. It leaps from the boiling water, and the cook tells it the heat is giving it flavor and making it food. Today's word.
screen: `THE CHICKPEA IN THE POT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: being cooked. Today, when the heat you named comes up, say the line once, and see if you can stay in the pot a little longer. Day two hundred seven.

208.title: Not the thing, my view
208.hook: if something outside pains you, it's your judgment of it, and that you can change (Meditations 8.47)
208.howItsDone: Readers of the Stoics often practice separating events from judgments, sometimes by writing down what happened and then the story they told about it; modern cognitive therapy draws on a similar idea.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chickpea in the pot, and the cook who said the heat was making it good. Your line was being cooked. Did you stay in the pot a little longer? Day two hundred eight.

It's raining on the day of the picnic. One person says: great, ruined. Another says: fine, we'll eat in the car, it'll be an adventure. Same rain. Same car. Or two people get the same curt email from the boss. One spends the evening furious. The other shrugs: she's probably slammed this week. The email didn't change. What changed was the story each of them told about it. Marcus spent his life trying to catch himself in that gap, between what happens and what we make of it. Today: not the thing, my view.
screen: `SAME RAIN, TWO PICNICS.` → `THE STORY WE TELL ABOUT IT.` → `NOT THE THING, MY VIEW.`

segments.voice: Here's how Book Eight, section forty-seven, begins in George Long's translation: "If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgement about it." And then: it's in your power to wipe out that judgment now. This is the heart of Stoic practice. Marcus had read Epictetus, the former slave turned teacher, and Epictetus said something very close: people are troubled not by things, but by their opinions about things. Now, let's be fair to the idea, because it's easy to hear it wrong. Marcus isn't saying pain is imaginary. A broken arm hurts. Grief is real. What he's pointing at is the second layer: the story on top. This shouldn't be happening. This always happens to me. This is a disaster. That layer is judgment, and judgment is yours to examine. And Marcus goes further in the same passage, which people often skip. If what bothers you is something in your own character, who's stopping you from correcting it? And if it's that you're not doing something you know is right, why not do it instead of complaining? And if something too strong for you really stands in the way, then don't grieve, because the cause isn't yours. So this isn't just changing your mind. It's a sorting. Some things you reframe. Some you act on. Some you let go. What you can almost always do is notice the story and ask whether it's true. Your line: not the thing, my view.
screen: `IT IS NOT THIS THING THAT DISTURBS THEE.` · `EPICTETUS: NOT THINGS, BUT OPINIONS.` · `REFRAME, ACT, OR LET GO.` · then, large: `NOT THE THING, MY VIEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rephrase one complaint. Settle, and let one small complaint come up. The traffic, a coworker, the weather. Say it inside the way you usually do. Then say it again, plainly, without the story: what actually happened? Then notice the judgment you added, and ask if it's true. Try one new sentence about it. The bell holds the time.
Not the thing. Marcus says when something outside pains you, it's your judgment about it that disturbs you, and that you can change. Today's word.
Your line: not the thing, my view. Today, catch one complaint as it comes out of your mouth, and rephrase it once. Day two hundred eight.

209.title: The bitter cucumber
209.hook: a cucumber is bitter? put it down; briars in the path? step aside (Meditations 8.50)
209.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this line for small daily irritations: deal with the thing simply, and skip the added complaint about why the world contains it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus said it's not the thing that disturbs you, but your judgment of it. Your line was not the thing, my view. Which complaint did you rephrase? Day two hundred nine.

You bite into a sandwich and the lettuce is gone slimy. You could put it down. Or you could hold it up and say to the room: why? Why does this always happen? Who packs a sandwich like this? What's wrong with this whole store? Five minutes later, you're still holding the sandwich. Some of us are very gifted at turning small annoyances into long speeches. Marcus, it seems, knew the habit. So he gave himself one of the shortest, driest bits of advice in the whole book. It starts with a vegetable. Today: the bitter cucumber.
screen: `THE SLIMY LETTUCE.` → `A LONG SPEECH ABOUT A SANDWICH.` → `THE BITTER CUCUMBER.`

segments.voice: Book Eight, section fifty, in George Long's translation: "A cucumber is bitter. Throw it away. There are briars in the road. Turn aside from them." Then Marcus says: this is enough. Don't add, and why were such things ever made? That's the whole trick. The first part is action. Bitter? Put it down. Thorny path? Go around. The second part is what not to add: the speech. The why me. The why is the world like this. Marcus even has a joke about it. If you asked why there are bitter cucumbers, he says, someone who understands nature would laugh at you. It would be like walking into a carpenter's shop and complaining about the wood shavings on the floor, or into a shoemaker's and complaining about the leather scraps. Of course there are scraps. That's what a workshop looks like when things are being made. For the Stoics, the world is nature's workshop, and bitter cucumbers and briars are some of the shavings. This connects to yesterday. Yesterday was about the judgment you add to a thing. Today is simpler. Some things don't even need a new judgment. They need a small movement: put it down, step aside, carry on. You don't have to understand why the cucumber is bitter. You don't have to fix the briars. You don't have to make it mean something about your life. There's a lightness to it, almost funny. Most annoyances are cucumbers. Your line: step aside.
screen: `BITTER? THROW IT AWAY.` · `DON'T ADD: WHY WAS THIS MADE?` · `SHAVINGS ON THE WORKSHOP FLOOR.` · then, large: `STEP ASIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: step around one annoyance. Settle, and let a small, familiar annoyance come to mind. The noisy neighbor, the slow app, the sock that's always inside out. Notice the speech that usually comes with it. Then picture yourself simply putting it down, or stepping around it, with no speech at all. Feel how light that is. Breathe there. The bell holds the time.
The bitter cucumber. Marcus says if a cucumber is bitter, throw it away; if there are briars in the road, turn aside, and don't ask why. Today's word.
Your line: step aside. Today, when a small annoyance shows up, handle it in one move, and skip the speech. Day two hundred nine.

210.title: The three fish
210.hook: as fishermen come, one fish leaves early, one plays dead, one is caught (Masnavi 4.2202ff)
210.howItsDone: This fable is told across many cultures, from the Panchatantra to Kalila and Dimna to Rumi; in Sufi teaching it is often read as a call to respond to the first stirrings of conscience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bitter cucumber: throw it away, step around the briars. Your line was step aside. Which speech did you skip? Day two hundred ten.

The check engine light comes on. You tell yourself you'll deal with it next week. The tooth that twinges when you drink something cold. The friend who's been quiet for a month. The small voice at work that says this project is heading for the rocks. Most trouble sends a warning first. The question is what we do in the gap between the warning and the net. Rumi tells an old story, one he found in a much older book of animal fables, about three fish in a lake, and the morning the fishermen came by. Today: the three fish.
screen: `THE CHECK ENGINE LIGHT.` → `BETWEEN THE WARNING AND THE NET.` → `THE THREE FISH.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Four of the Masnavi. In a lake lived three fish: one wise, one half-wise, and one foolish. One day some fishermen walk past, notice the fish, and hurry off to get their net. The wise fish sees it and decides right then: I'm leaving. The lake connects to the sea, the way is hard, but it goes at once. And Rumi adds a detail. It doesn't stop to consult the others, because they'd talk it out of going. Home is comfortable, and comfort is persuasive. So it makes the long trip alone and reaches the open sea. The half-wise fish waits. When the fishermen come back with the net, it's too late to leave, and it's sorry it didn't go with its friend. But it has one good idea. It plays dead, and floats belly up on the water. The fisherman picks it up, thinks, a dead fish, and tosses it aside. And it slips, quietly, back into the water and gets away. The foolish fish does neither. It thrashes around in panic, jumping this way and that, and the net closes on it. That evening, it's in the frying pan. The story came to Rumi from Kalila and Dimna, a book of fables with roots in the ancient Indian Panchatantra. Rumi reads it his own way. The wise fish is the soul that acts on the first sign, before the net arrives. The half-wise one survives by a kind of dying, like the parrot a few weeks ago. The foolish one waits and flails. Your line: leave in time.
